newsitem.title: ISRAEL: PLO says summit with Netanyahu a turning point.
newsitem.headline: PLO says summit with Netanyahu a turning point.

text.p: Yasser Arafat nearly stormed out of a summit with Israel's Benjamin Netanyahu on Tuesday but Palestinians at the meeting called the day the start of what could be a beautiful relationship.

"This meeting was a positive turning point in the personal relationship between Netanyahu and Arafat," Mohammad Dahlan, head of Palestinian preventive security in the self-ruled Gaza Strip, told Reuters.

The summit between Palestinian President Arafat and Prime Minister Netanyahu failed to wrap up a deal to give Palestinians self-rule in the West Bank town of Hebron but U.S. special envoy Dennis Ross reported "real progress".

The right-wing Netanyahu had for weeks after his election in May resisted even meeting the guerrilla-turned-peacemaker but on Tuesday he and Arafat met for 3-1/2 hours at the Israeli border with Gaza.

"Let me say this was a very, very good meeting between the two leaders," said Ross, who at times joined them. Palestinians who took part agreed with the assessment but told of Arafat throwing another one of what they called his classic tantrums.

Witnesses said the dispute emerged over security plans for Hebron, including whether Israel alone or together with the Palestinians would patrol near the holiest site, the tomb of the biblical Abraham, known to Moslems as al-Ibrahimi mosque.

"Arafat was screaming, 'If you want to control al-Ibrahimi mosque, take the mosque, take everything. Take Hebron, I don't want it. You don't want an agreement on Hebron. You don't want to agree on anything'," said a PLO official who declined to be identified.

"And he walked towards the door and he was about to reach for the doorknob when Dahlan and Major-General Abdel-Razak al-Yahya grabbed Arafat and tried to persuade him not to leave the room," the official said.

"They called on Dennis Ross to help them keep him from leaving and Netanyahu's face was red. He was, I think, perplexed and amazed at what he was seeing but he was very calm. And then Arafat cooled down and then it happened again," he said.
"We pleaded with Arafat to stay and continue the talks. Despite this the talks with Netanyahu were very good. Netanyahu was more understanding of the agreement," the official said.
Another official quoted Netanyahu as telling Arafat: "I understand your feelings, your emotions. I respect that."

"Then Arafat calmed down and apologised for the outburst and told Netanyahu: 'You have to understand the religious attachment and my feelings.' And Netanyahu responded: 'I respect that'," the official said.
Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat called the atmosphere "very productive". A senior Israeli official briefing reporters said he believed a deal would be signed within a week.
Arafat refused to say a word when he left the meeting but smiled when he waved to reporters.
